idiom_name: View interface + Presenter struct (consumer-defined interface, injected view)
implementation_notes: Go has no classes; the view contract becomes a small interface usually declared next to the presenter (the consumer defines the interface it needs), the presenter is a struct holding that interface plus the model, and wiring happens in a constructor or in main. Nothing needs to replace the classic structure: Go's implicit interface satisfaction means the concrete screen declares no conformance, and a test double is a five-line struct or a function-backed type, which is why the full structure is cheap to hand-write. Keep the classic form wherever the screen has logic worth testing without the widget toolkit; plain handlers suffice for trivial HTTP or CLI screens. Method values and small function-typed fields are the idiomatic alternative to a view interface when the view contract is one or two callbacks.
pitfalls: Interface satisfaction is implicit, so renaming or extending a method silently detaches the real view; keep the interface minimal and assert conformance at compile time.
Inject the view as an interface value holding a pointer: a struct view passed by value is copied and the presenter then drives a different copy than the one on screen.
Most Go GUI bindings (GTK, Fyne) require widget access on the main thread; a presenter invoked from a goroutine must marshal through a channel, glib idle callback or the toolkit's dispatcher.
